In a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometer, a change in the field's direction by 90 degrees is necessary for sensing magnetic fields, as the signal is proportional to the difference in phases experienced by two atomic paths. However, by using Raman transitions to generate atomic rabattals in a triangular configuration, it is possible to measure local magnetic fields along the sensing coil's direction. This approach allows for the detection of fields as small as $10^{-14}$ Tesla/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ through fluctuations, and $10^{-12}$ Tesla through static fields, surpassing the quantum limit in the sensitivity measurement.

On the basis of a theoretical model that incorporates spin--orbit coupling, we investigate the behavior of a single atomic layer of a heavy fermion system, specifically the structure of adatoms or dimers that are magnetic and their interaction with the system. The unaltered sublattice of the adatom/dimer layer is treated as a potential that influences the local and long-range arrangements of the remaining, unconventional superconducting (SC) YSr states. Without loss of generality, we utilize a tight-binding framework to describe the electron movement within the adatom/dimer layer and the underlying heavy fermion system. The critical component in determining the energy spectrum of the YSr states is the SC order parameter, which can either be uniform or layered and may require special calculation in certain scenarios. In the case of the heavy fermion system CeRu$_4$P$_8$, we use experimental data to define the SC order parameter. Through the integration of the local SC order parameter and the potential created by the adatom/dimer, we obtain the distribution of YSr states, which can appear as peaks in the density of states or as gaps in the spectrum, contingent upon the adatom/dimer configuration and the presence of spin--orbit coupling. The analysis of the nodeless even-parity $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave SC model reveals identical $k$-dependent order parameters for all possible $q$ values within the layered SC system. In a

Deep convolutional neural networks have achieved remarkable success in image classification tasks, but their performance can be inconsistent when trained with limited label data and prone to overfitting. To address this, ensemble methods have been explored, where multiple base classifiers are trained on different subsets of data and combined to produce the final classification. In the context of image classification, ensemble methods can be particularly effective when combining residual and convolutional layers in a deep neural network architecture. Our research involves training an ensemble of 50 base classifiers on different subsets of data, each consisting of a small number of labels, and then combining their outputs to achieve the highest accuracy. Compared to a single, fully trained convolutional neural network, our ensemble approach yields significant improvements in classification accuracy on both Caltech-UCS and Stanford cars datasets. On the Caltech-UCS dataset, our method achieves an average precision of 93.1% versus 79.5% for a single network, while on the Stanford cars dataset, our method achieves an average precision of 89.4% versus 78.3% for a single network.

This research focuses on the universal correction components of wide-range, generalized parton cascades, specifically for transverse gauge bosons (W, Z) within the framework of leading-order QCD. The approach involves integrating universal correction PDFs, which account for hard splittings and collinear losses, into generalized parton cascade models. The description of universal correction PDFs for transverse gauge bosons (W, Z) transversely to their direction of motion, relative to the colliding partons, utilizes the same framework as for transverse jets. The implementation of these universal correction PDFs, denoted as AnkleOS, is available within the PYTHIA event generator. The research also includes the distribution functions for transverse gluons, antisymmetric quarks, and asymmetric quark splittings as additional components of the AnkleOS package. In 1931, Kurt Godel's incompleteness theorem highlighted the fundamental limitations of formalized theories, revealing the existence of true but unprovable statements within these systems. Over a decade later, J Barkley Rosser built upon Godel's work, further refining these boundaries. Rosser's theorem reveals that within any formalized system S similar to Peano arithmetic, there is no provable statement that is true for all possible values of the system's index function. In the realm of formal systems centered around arithmetic, this characterization stands as an unbreachable logical chasm. Through the application of Rosser's strengthening of the first incompleteness theorem, researchers have gained profound insights into the nature of consistency statements within these systems. In particular, this strengthened principle enables the derivation of a theorem originally proved by Solomon Feferman in 1960, which demonstrates that within any formalized system akin to Peano arithmetic, there exists a true statement that asserts the system's own consistency.

The paper at hand focuses on linear systems described by differential equations of integer order and extends previous work on linear subspaces that remain within the system's behavior when the system transitions from integer order to fractional order. A key aspect of the paper establishes that linear subspaces are invariant in fractional order systems under the same conditions that ensure their invariance in integer order systems. Additionally, the paper provides a direct method for determining invariant linear subspaces within the context of fractional order systems.

The paper resolves uniqueness issues in an inverse problem for a heat equation that involves determining the source term within a domain in Euclidean space. Unique solutions can be found for variables representing the initial mass of a substance in a domain and a neighboring annulus, given partial measurements of the substance's heat over time from the outside. The approach involves logarithmic slope restrictions in the measurable output data and the use of Carleman-type operators due to observability inequalities for the associated wave equation. A key factor in the proof is the ability to relate the observability inequality's weak form to a strong form through the Banach-Tarski decomposition.

We introduce a minimal dark radiation component to explain the observed dark energy fraction, and incorporate a dark sector that is invariant under a discrete symmetry known as dark parity. This minimal setup extends the standard model particle content and involves three right-handed neutrinos to achieve neutrino mass through a modified, radiation-type seesaw framework. The dark parity symmetry ensures the stability of dark matter and dark radiation, and eliminates lepton number non-conserving processes. However, due to the linearized instability of vacuum in the dark sector, we use a two-component dark sector model with one heavy, dark neutrino mediating interactions between the two sectors. The implementation of dark parity as a Z2 x Z2 symmetry, results in two distinct representations for the left-handed and right-handed dark neutrino generations, leading to different mass eigenstates and the possibility of dark antimatter formation. The parameter space is constrained using big bang nucleosynthesis predictions, dark matter relic density, and the absence of dark antimatter, as well as the decay length of heavy dark neutrinos. The consistency of the models is further verified by ensuring the stability of the vacuum in the dark sector through the Casimir effect, and the feasibility of dark parity symmetry is confirmed through the absence of parity-violating processes.
